beats.narration_text: Hello, I'm Vineet S.. Prioritizing A I features is harder than prioritizing normal features. Some ideas sound great and cannot be built well. Others work in a demo and cost too much at scale. Here is how product managers weigh it.

props.segment: How to Prioritize AI Product Features
props.command: How do I prioritize features on an AI product roadmap?
output: Cost, latency and quality shape the scope
Risk and business impact break ties

beats.narration_text: The best AI feature is the one customers value, and we can ship well. Impressive is not the same as valuable, and valuable is not the same as feasible. The roadmap lives where those overlap.

props.text:
The best AI feature is
the most impressive
one to demo.
props.triggerWords: the most impressive, one to demo
props.replacementWords: the one customers value, and we can ship well

beats.narration_text: Here are the eight factors, in six groups. Customer value. AI feasibility. Engineering effort. Model quality. Cost and latency. And risk and business impact. No single one decides. The skill is weighing them together.

Start with value. How big is the customer problem, and how often does it happen? Then feasibility. Can today's models do this reliably? A quick prototype on real data answers that faster than a debate. If quality is not close, the feature is a research bet, not a roadmap item.

layers.title: AI feasibility
layers.sub: Can today's models do it reliably?

layers.title: Not close? Research bet
layers.sub: Keep it off the committed roadmap

beats.narration_text: Next, effort and quality. Engineering effort covers integration, data and evaluation work, not only the model call. Model quality asks how good the feature must be to be useful. A writing helper can be wrong sometimes. A medical or legal feature cannot. Set the quality bar from the use case.

props.arcCaption: For example: writing helper versus legal advice
props.settleLine: Set the bar from the use case

beats.narration_text: Then cost and latency. Every request costs money, and a feature used a million times a day can become expensive fast. Latency matters too. People wait a second for a search, but not twenty seconds for a suggestion. If the cost or delay breaks the experience, shrink the feature or choose a smaller model.

layers.title: Latency budget
layers.sub: How long will users really wait?

layers.title: Margin check
layers.sub: Does it still pay at full scale?

layers.title: Too heavy? Shrink it
layers.sub: Smaller scope or a smaller model

beats.narration_text: Now risk and business impact. Risk covers wrong answers, privacy, safety and reputation. Higher risk needs more testing and human review, which adds effort. Business impact asks what moves revenue, retention or cost. A modest feature with clear impact often beats a flashy one without it.

Put it together. Score each idea on value, feasibility, effort, cost and risk. Prototype the uncertain ones before you commit. Sequence quick wins first, then bigger bets once you have learned. And revisit often, because models, prices and capabilities keep changing.

layers.title: Quick wins first
layers.sub: Bigger bets once you have learned

beats.narration_text: So, prioritizing. Start with value and feasibility. Check effort, quality, cost and latency. Weigh risk and impact. And revisit the roadmap as models change.
